glossary.title: Backgammon terms
glossary.intro: The words this app uses for things, and what they mean at the board.
glossary.point.body: The twenty-four narrow triangles. A point with two or more of your checkers on it is yours — your opponent cannot land there. Most of backgammon is a fight over which of them you each hold.
glossary.pip.body: One step. Your pip count is the total number of steps all fifteen of your checkers still have to travel to get home, so the lower it is the further ahead you are in the race.
glossary.blot.body: A single checker alone on a point. It can be hit, which sends it back to the very start, so leaving one is a risk you take on purpose or not at all.
glossary.hit.body: Landing on a lone opposing checker and sending it to the bar. It costs your opponent every step that checker had already travelled, which is why a hit deep in your home board hurts so much.
glossary.bar.body: The raised divider down the middle. A checker that has been hit sits there, and its owner may do nothing else until it re-enters on the far side of the board.
glossary.anchor.body: Two or more of your checkers held on a point inside your opponent’s home board. It gives a hit checker somewhere safe to land, and it is why being behind is not the same as being lost.
glossary.prime.body: A wall of consecutive points you hold. Six in a row cannot be jumped by any roll at all, so anything of your opponent’s trapped behind it stays trapped.
glossary.backgame.body: Deliberately holding two anchors deep in your opponent’s home board and waiting. You give up the race entirely and play for the one shot that turns the game round.
glossary.gammon.body: Winning before your opponent has borne a single checker off. It is worth two points instead of one, which is why a hopeless-looking position is still worth playing out.
glossary.backgammon.body: Winning while your opponent still has a checker on the bar or in your home board. Three points, and rare enough to be worth remembering.
glossary.cube.body: Either player may offer to double the stake before their roll. The other must take it — and own the cube, so only they can double next — or give up the game immediately for what it is currently worth. It is where most matches are actually won and lost.
glossary.crawford.body: The one game after either player reaches match point is played without the cube. It stops a player who is behind from doubling immediately every game with nothing to lose.
glossary.match.body: A match runs until someone reaches the target number of points, not for a fixed number of games. Longer matches favour the better player, because luck has more time to even out.
glossary.pr.body: Performance rating: the average equity your play throws away per decision, measured against the engine’s best. Lower is better, it does not care whether you won, and it is the only number here that measures you rather than the dice.
